description: Mitad ingeniería, mitad caos, 100% NASA Space Apps Challenge. Si la app no despega, al menos el grupo sí. 💀🚀
summary:
Rocket Fleet 11 is a free, browser-based game that turns NASA missions into hands-on engineering practice. Players build a rocket part by part under a budget cap, check that every part and system fits together, and launch it in a physics simulation where gravity, drag, Max-Q and staging decide the outcome. When a flight fails, the mission report explains the physical cause, so failure becomes the lesson.

Levels progress from a suborbital hop to a crewed Moon mission inspired by Artemis, where players face real problems from NASA history: Apollo 6 pogo oscillation, the Apollo 11 1202 alarm, Apollo 13 and the Artemis I heat shield. A team mode splits players into builders and ground control, with GO/NO-GO reviews and ground tasks based on real launch rules.

It addresses Space Mission Design Game. It matters because students rarely get to practice the trade-offs engineers face every day. Rocket Fleet 11 runs in any browser, in English and Spanish, with no installation.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Rocket Fleet 11 is an educational space-mission design game. Players design a rocket within a fixed budget, launch it in a physics simulation, and learn from a report that explains why the mission succeeded or failed. Five levels go from a tutorial to a crewed Moon mission. A free mode allows open experimentation, and a team mode recreates the roles of builders and mission control.

HOW IT WORKS

The rocket is built on a free blueprint. Every joint is checked for compatibility (fuel feed, mechanical load, staging), and live "status lights" show budget, thrust-to-weight ratio, stability (center of gravity vs. center of pressure) and fairing fit. The flight is a 2D numerical simulation around Earth with gravity, an exponential atmosphere, aerodynamic drag, dynamic pressure (Max-Q), staging and automatic guidance. Whether the rocket reaches orbit is decided by the physics, not by random rolls. In team mode, two browser windows communicate in real time: ground control chooses the launch base and window, solves ground tasks (weather rules, range safety, countdown order, antenna tracking) and gives GO/NO-GO, while builders hold the key technical facts.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

It turns watching a launch into practicing engineering: trade-offs under a budget, interfaces between systems, and learning from failure. A "Student" mode explains concepts in plain words; an "Engineer" mode adds the formulas and the math for every part (62 reference cards). It runs on low-end school computers and is free, so the cost of reaching one more student is close to zero.

TOOLS AND LANGUAGES

HTML, CSS and JavaScript (no frameworks), Canvas 2D graphics, the BroadcastChannel API for team mode, a Python build script that bundles everything into one ~420 KB file, Playwright for automated end-to-end testing, Google Fonts, and Vercel for hosting. We used Claude (Anthropic), an AI assistant, for coding and debugging, research, writing, English translation, slide design and logo design. The team defined the concept, the requirements and the game design, reviewed and tested every version, and made all final decisions.

CREATIVITY

It combines the budget puzzles of bridge-building games with rocket engineering, and adds mission-control teamwork and real historical incidents as decision points, including the same test-flight decision NASA made for Artemis.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Accessibility (high-legibility font, color contrast, keyboard shortcuts), school hardware (one small file, no installation), language (full English/Spanish switch), honesty of the physics (we removed an unreliable estimate so only the simulation decides), and real-world rules such as mandatory flight termination systems and launch weather criteria (simplified).
